confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

(Serie de vocabularios y diccionarios indígenas "Mariano Silva y Aceves" 29.) México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. xii+209 pp; Tercera parte 'La gramática mixteca', pp. 145-178. catalog_locator: Tercera parte 'La gramática mixteca', 0. La fonología, sec. 0.1.10 'Las vocales dobles' and sec. 0.2 'Los tonos', p. 147 (p. 160 of the archive.org facsimile)
catalog_quote: 0.1.10. Las vocales dobles. La mayoría de las palabras del mixteco son de dos sílabas y la primera de éstas es la tónica. Algunas palabras constan de una consonante seguida de vocal doble. Se considera que las palabras con vocal doble son de dos sílabas. La primera sílaba consta de una consonante más una vocal, mientras que la segunda sílaba consta de una sola vocal. Nótese los siguientes ejemplos: saa pájaro tsaa nuevo. 0.2. Los tonos. Las palabras mixtecas se diferencian de las palabras castellanas en que cada sílaba tiene su propio tono. Hay tres tonos distintos, que son: alto, medio, y bajo. Estos tres tonos corresponden, más o menos, a las notas musicales sol, mi y do.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Most Mixtec words have two syllables, and the first of these is the stressed (tonic) one. Some words consist of a consonant followed by a double vowel. Words with a double vowel are considered to have two syllables: the first syllable consists of a consonant plus a vowel, while the second consists of a vowel alone. [...] 0.2 Tones. Mixtec words differ from Spanish words in that every syllable has its own tone. There are three distinct tones: high, mid and low.
new_statements.citation: Stark Campbell, Sara, Andrea Johnson Peterson y Filiberto Lorenzo Cruz (comps.). 1986. Diccionario mixteco de San Juan Colorado. (Serie de vocabularios y diccionarios indígenas "Mariano Silva y Aceves" 29.) México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (225 pp. archive.org facsimile, image-only) + archive.org scanned). I rendered p. 160 (printed p. 147, running head 'LA FONOLOGIA 0.2') and read it as an image: sec. '0.1.10. Las vocales dobles' reads exactly 'La mayoria de las palabras del mixteco son de dos silabas y la primera de estas es la tonica. Algunas palabras constan de una consonante seguida de vocal doble. Se considera que las palabras con vocal doble son de dos silabas. La primera silaba consta de una consonante mas una vocal, mientras que la segunda silaba consta de una sola vocal. Notese los siguientes ejemplos: saa pajaro, tsaa nuevo', followed by '0.2. Los tonos.. cada silaba tiene su propio tono. Hay tres ton…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the canonical disyllabic word (the Mixtec couplet, including CVV words analysed as CV.V), stress falls on the first syllable, i.e. the penultimate syllable / couplet-initial syllable; the language additionally has three contrastive level tones (high, mid, low) on every syllable, written with acute/grave accents (accents mark tone, not stress).
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning stress. The sketch says nothing about words longer than two syllables (prefixed verbs, compounds) or enclitics; it separately notes (0.2.4, pp. 148-149) that in medio-alto words whose first syllable ends in h the first vowel is lengthened (yoohó 'tú'), a lengthening that disappears when the tone changes — described as a tonal effect, not as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for disyllabic (couplet) words in a practical grammar sketch appended to an SIL bilingual dictionary; for disyllables 'first syllable' = penult = couplet-initial, so the reading fixed: penultimate syllable is chosen on the pan-Mixtec couplet-stress interpretation (could equally be filed as couplet-initial). Tone language (3 levels); no instrumental evidence given.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes exactly 'el mixteco de San Juan Colorado, distrito de Jamiltepec, Oaxaca' (Mixteca de la Costa) = Glottolog sanj1281 / ISO mjc; authors are the SIL team for this variety (Sharon Stark = Sara Stark Campbell, Audrey F. Johnson = Andrea Johnson Peterson). No dialect mismatch.

Language Dynamics and Change 14(1): 1-41. doi:10.1163/22105832-bja10031 (green OA: repository copy doi:10.48620/96643). tone_statements.quote: San Juan Colorado Mixtec The data for this variety comes from Stark et al. (1986). Tones are marked throughout (MULG). This variety has three level tones (low, mid, high), but the combination of low-high is not attested, resulting in 8 contrastive tone melodies. The final glottal stop does not affect tones in this variety, producing the familiar mergers. The reflexes of *HL and *LH sets are very interesting. *LH has mid-mid reflex, merging these sets with the *HH and *HHʔ ones. The numerals show different reflexes from other *LL sets, namely mid-mid.
tone_statements.locator: Supplementary Material 'Standardization of tone notations', Group 2, section 'San Juan Colorado Mixtec', p. 4 (with Table 5, p. 4)
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (L, M, H), one tone per vowel/mora of the disyllabic couplet, 8 contrastive couplet melodies (L-H absent); glottal stop does not interact with tone; lexical tone data only (no stress statement).

Guildford: Surrey Morphology Group, University of Surrey. doi:10.15126/SMG.28/1.06. Language page 'San Juan Colorado Mixtec' (Facts, Sources of the data, Orthography, Tones, Verbal inflection) + 237-verb paradigm table with tone digits.
tone_statements.quote: San Juan Colorado Mixtec has three level tones. To facilitate comparison we have converted the orthography of the original, which uses diacritics, to numbers: 1 (low), 2 (mid) and 3 (high). Like in other Mixtec languages, tonal word phonology is organized in melodies. Bimoraic words have the following melodies. /3-3/ sɨ³vɨ³ ‘name’ [...] /1-1/ ko¹o¹ ‘snake’ [...] Tone plays a fundamental role in the realization of such forms. The tonal melody of the CPL could be taken as being lexical, and for most verbs, the IRR does not change tone (although there are exceptions dividing the verbs into tone classes). However, the INCPL differs from the CPL (except for some irregular verbs)
tone_statements.locator: OMICD language page Info/MJC, sections 'Tones' and 'Verbal inflection'
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (1 low, 2 mid, 3 high) on each mora, seven attested bimoraic melodies, plus grammatical tone: incompletive aspect formed from the completive by tone change (verb tone classes).

tone_statements.citation: Johnson, Audrey F., Filiberto Lorenzo C. & Sharon Stark. 1983. Cuhva cahvi yo tsa cahan vaha [Leyendo y escribiendo en mixteco] (mixteco de San Juan Colorado). [1a ed.] México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 34 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 12477 (PDF online at SIL); also reproduced on the community site sanjuancolorado.net ('Aprende Mixteco' page + PDF). Tone: Lección Dos 'Signos del tiempo de los verbos' and Lección Nueve.
tone_statements.quote: Muchos pares de palabras en mixteco varían solo por los tonos. Es decir, se escriben con las mismas letras, pero la voz sube o baja de una manera diferente en cada palabra para darle el significado correcto. Casi siempre las palabras que se leen antes y después de una palabra dan a entender que palabra es. Sin embargo, los tiempos de algunos verbos se denotan sólo por el tono, por eso, los diferenciamos con un acento (ꞌ) y una rayita (_). Un acento escrito en la última vocal del verbo indica tiempo presente. Una rayita escrita debajo de la última vocal del verbo significa tiempo pasado. Ejemplos: Tiempo Presente Tiempo Pasado Jatá ña Ella está comprando Jata̱ ña Ella Compró
tone_statements.translation: Many word pairs in Mixtec differ only in their tones. That is, they are written with the same letters, but the voice rises or falls differently in each word to give it the right meaning. Almost always the words read before and after a word make clear which word it is. However, the tenses of some verbs are marked only by tone, so we distinguish them with an accent and a small underline. An accent written on the last vowel of the verb indicates present tense. An underline written under the last vowel of the verb means past tense. Examples: Present / Past: Jatá ña 'she is buying' / Jata̱ ña 'she bought'.
tone_statements.locator: 'Aprende Mixteco' page, Lección Dos 'Signos del Tiempo de los Verbos' (= primer 'Leyendo y Escribiendo en Mixteco')
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone (tone-only minimal pairs) and grammatical tone distinguishing present vs past on verbs; orthography marks tone only on verbs (acute = present, underline = past); no inventory stated.
